paragraphs: A temporal pattern depends on how a signal unfolds, so its meaning cannot always be read from a single instant. This paper proposes a neural architecture in which the changing state of the nodes carries information about earlier input. Time is represented through the network’s ongoing dynamics, allowing present responses to depend on temporal context.

The authors contrast this approach with making additional copies of network components to represent different times. Their concrete example adds capacitive inputs to an otherwise standard back-propagation model. These inputs act as temporal feature detectors: they let the network respond to features of a signal’s evolution rather than only to its current value.

Experiments on motion detection and word discrimination illustrate features of the architecture. Both tasks make temporal context relevant, connecting the design to recognizable processing problems. The contribution is a way to incorporate time into the behavior of network components while retaining a familiar learning framework. The paper also discusses possible extensions of that architecture.
neurips-1987-a-dynamical-approach-to-tem.tldr: The paper represents temporal context through changing neural states and demonstrates capacitive temporal feature detectors within a back-propagation network.

paragraphs: The paper connects a biological theory of visual development with the design of artificial neural networks. Its starting point is an earlier account of how a single cortical cell develops selectivity and ocular dominance. These properties concern which visual inputs a cell responds to and how strongly it favors input from one eye. That account had already been extended to a network for layer IV of visual cortex.

The authors introduce a mean field approximation to make the network theory easier to understand. The purpose of this approximation is to capture the network’s behavior through a more manageable description. The abstract reports that it preserves quantitative results of the network theory while presenting them in a relatively transparent form.

The paper then applies the theory to artificial neural networks and reports a substantial reduction in architectural complexity. This connects the simplification of a biological model to the possibility of simpler artificial designs. The central contribution is therefore both explanatory and architectural: a more accessible description of collective neural behavior that can inform network construction.
neurips-1987-a-mean-field-theory-of-laye.tldr: A mean field approximation simplifies a visual-cortex network theory and supports less complex artificial neural architectures.

paragraphs: This paper describes neural networks that learn backgammon from positions evaluated by a human expert. Training is supervised: the expert’s judgments provide the examples the networks learn to reproduce. The task therefore tests whether a network can absorb useful knowledge about a game from a collection of evaluated situations.

The networks reach an intermediate-to-advanced level of play. Matches against humans and conventional computer programs provide evidence that the learned knowledge transfers to actual play. The authors interpret this as substantial generalization from expert examples: the training supports useful decisions in the broader setting of a match.

The study also uses backgammon to examine practical learning questions. These include how to encode positions efficiently, organize training, handle real-valued inputs and outputs, scale the approach, and escape local minima during learning. Together, these issues connect representation and optimization to playing ability. The stated result shows that supervised expert knowledge can support meaningful game performance, with potential applications discussed for games and other domains.
neurips-1987-a-neural-network-that-learn.tldr: Networks trained on expert-evaluated positions generalize well enough to play backgammon at an intermediate-to-advanced level.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a neural network needs more connections per neuron to handle a more complex problem. It measures connectivity by the number of synapses per neuron and problem complexity through entropy. The question links a physical feature of a network’s architecture to an information-based description of what it must learn.

Ordinary switching theory initially suggests that no such connection is necessary. Any Boolean function can be constructed using components with very few inputs, such as two-input NAND gates. From the perspective of implementing a function, low connectivity therefore appears compatible with arbitrarily varied computational tasks.

The paper proves a different result when the network must learn from examples using a local learning rule: the problem’s entropy provides a lower bound on connectivity. The learning assumptions are essential to the claim. A circuit’s ability to express a function does not by itself establish that a locally trained network can learn it with equally sparse connections. The result makes learning procedure and architecture part of the same theoretical question.
neurips-1987-connectivity-versus-entropy.tldr: For networks learning from examples through local rules, problem entropy imposes a lower bound on connectivity.

paragraphs: Neural optimization systems often need to improve an objective while keeping their outputs within a set of valid solutions. Adding a quadratic penalty for invalid outputs is one common approach. The paper explains that this does not guarantee constraint satisfaction when other forces influence the network or several constraints interact.

The proposed basic differential multiplier method introduces neurons that estimate Lagrange multipliers. These estimates generate forces that progressively enforce the constraints as the network evolves. The method turns the numerical method of multipliers into a continuous dynamical process, making constraint enforcement an active part of the network’s behavior.

The authors prove local convergence of the differential equations to a constrained minimum and state that the method satisfies constraints exactly. Local convergence concerns behavior near the relevant solution; it does not establish convergence from every starting point. Applications include producing valid permutation codewords in analog decoding and valid traveling-salesman tours. In both settings, the method addresses the need for an optimized answer to obey the rules that make it usable.
neurips-1987-constrained-differential-op.tldr: The differential multiplier method uses evolving multiplier neurons to enforce constraints exactly, with a proof of local convergence to a constrained minimum.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a visual system can recover three-dimensional structure from motion. The underlying challenge is to use changes in what is seen to understand the spatial arrangement producing those changes. The authors frame this ability as important to both human and non-human primates, connecting a computational problem with a biological function.

Their approach uses a parallel-processing model to explore how the biological visual system might perform this task. Parallel processing provides the organizing framework for the proposed explanation. The model is used to investigate a possible account of structure recovery, placing the emphasis on how a collection of processing operations could support visual interpretation.

The work also considers how a neurophysiologist could understand the biological solution. This gives the model a second role: it helps frame the scientific problem of explaining the mechanism behind the ability. The contribution described in the abstract is exploratory, linking a computational treatment of motion-based perception to questions about how that computation could be understood in primate vision.
neurips-1987-discovering-structure-from-.tldr: A parallel-processing model explores how primate vision might recover three-dimensional structure from motion.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a distributed neural model of the vestibulo-ocular system. Its goal is to explain the system’s response characteristics while representing anatomical and physiological observations more accurately. The model focuses on how signals about head motion pass through sensory cells and the neurons that receive their input.

Head motion is represented topographically by hair cells in the semicircular canals, meaning that spatial organization is part of the sensory description. Their signals are processed through multiple synapses in primary afferent neurons. These neurons exhibit a continuum of different dynamics, so the population contains varied temporal responses rather than a single common response type.

The authors apply the idea of multilayered neural networks to findings from the bullfrog vestibular nerve. This supports a mathematical description of an assembly whose physiological behavior varies with its anatomical properties. The approach matters because it treats that variation as part of the computation being explained. Distributed processing provides a framework for relating the organization of the sensory pathway to the behavior of the neuronal population.
neurips-1987-distributed-neural-informat.tldr: A multilayered model links anatomical variation to distributed processing of head-motion signals in the vestibular pathway.

paragraphs: Recognizing an object becomes harder when its image changes size or orientation. This paper presents a system for two-dimensional recognition that combines a complex-log conformal mapping with a distributed associative memory. The mapping and memory work together so that an object can be recognized despite changes in rotation or scale.

The recalled information serves several purposes. It provides an object classification, reconstructs the stored version of the object, and estimates how much the observed image has rotated or changed in size. Recognition therefore produces both an identity and information about the relationship between the current image and the memorized reference.

Experiments with real grayscale images demonstrate the feasibility of the approach. The abstract also reports resistance to moderate noise and occlusion, meaning that some image corruption or partial hiding can be tolerated. The significance is the combination of recognition, reconstruction, and transformation estimation within one memory-based system. Its stated robustness extends beyond clean transformed images, while remaining qualified by the moderate level of disturbance described.
neurips-1987-invariant-object-recognitio.tldr: A transformed-image associative memory recognizes rotated or rescaled objects while reconstructing stored images and estimating the transformations.

paragraphs: Recirculation learns a hidden representation by asking whether it can reproduce the original visible activity. Groups of nonlinear units form a closed loop, allowing activity to travel from the visible group through a hidden group and back. Learning aims to reduce the discrepancy between the starting visible vector and its reconstruction.

The procedure uses two passes around the loop. The first carries the original visible vector. The second carries a mixture of that original vector and the reconstruction. Each connection changes according to the activity on its sending side multiplied by the difference between its receiving unit’s activities on the two passes.

This rule turns changes in local activity into a learning signal, and the authors describe it as substantially simpler to implement than back-propagation. Simulations in simple networks usually find good codes quickly. The mathematical analysis establishes gradient descent on squared reconstruction error only in certain restricted cases. Together, these results support recirculation as a practical representation-learning procedure while identifying the narrower setting in which its optimization behavior is formally established.
neurips-1987-learning-representations-by.tldr: Recirculation learns hidden codes from activity differences across two passes through a loop, with gradient-descent guarantees in restricted cases.

paragraphs: The paper examines special-purpose chips for implementing connectionist neural networks in tasks such as pattern recognition and classification. Its focus is the hardware organization needed to make these networks useful in practice. The authors discuss why neural computation motivates dedicated designs and present three different ways to organize the required operations.

One design is a programmable connection matrix combining digital and analog elements. Another is an analog connection matrix whose connection strengths can be adjusted. The third is a digital best-match chip with pipelined processing. These alternatives cover different hardware arrangements for representing connections and carrying out operations relevant to neural processing.

The shared design principle is to distribute arithmetic processing among the places where data is stored. This arrangement aims to reduce data movement by bringing computation closer to the information it uses. That common principle ties the three designs together despite their different analog and digital choices. The paper’s contribution is an implementation perspective in which the placement of storage and arithmetic is central to supporting neural-network applications.
neurips-1987-microelectronic-implementat.tldr: Three specialized chip designs reduce data movement by distributing neural-network arithmetic among data storage.

paragraphs: Back-propagation is often used to reduce a least-squares difference between a network’s output and a teacher signal. This paper generalizes that choice of error measure using Minkowski-r power metrics. The parameter r changes how discrepancies are combined, allowing the learning objective to express different notions of a good match.

At r equal to two, the procedure recovers standard back-propagation. Smaller values approximate a city-block measure, while large values approach a measure governed by the largest discrepancy. Changing r therefore changes which patterns of error receive emphasis during learning, even though the overall approach remains based on gradient descent.

The authors describe an implementation and report experiments indicating that different values of r suit different purposes. Potential uses include reducing the influence of noisy outliers, forming more compact clusters, and matching the statistics of a domain. They also discuss error measures that may better reflect perception in speech or vision. The finding supports treating the error metric as a meaningful modeling choice rather than assuming that squared error fits every task.
neurips-1987-minkowski-r-back-propagatio.tldr: Minkowski-r back-propagation varies the error metric to adapt learning to noise, clustering goals, and domain characteristics.

paragraphs: This paper presents ways to estimate three requirements of a neural network: the range of functions its architecture can implement, the precision needed in its connections, and the number of training examples needed for reliable generalization. These questions concern what a network can represent, how accurately it must be realized, and how much evidence it needs to learn.

Counting implementable functions gives a measure of architectural generality. Estimating analog precision addresses a different aspect of the same design: how finely connection values need to be specified. Considering both quantities makes the network’s computational possibilities and its numerical requirements explicit parts of the analysis.

The third estimate concerns training data and the expectation that learning will extend beyond the examples observed. This places generalization alongside architecture and connection precision as a quantity to assess when studying a network. The contribution is a framework for estimating these three aspects of network capability and requirements, helping distinguish expressive possibilities from the practical demands of representing and learning them.
neurips-1987-network-generality-training.tldr: The paper estimates a network’s representational range, required connection precision, and training-data needs for reliable generalization.

paragraphs: The paper describes two ways to implement neural-network simulations on the Connection Machine. Its single-instruction, multiple-data parallelism lets many processors apply the same operation to different pieces of data. The authors use this organization to construct simulations with relatively simple data structures and control.

Both approaches support parallel evaluation of nonlinear functions, parallel updates to connection weights, and parallel propagation of activations and errors. They also allow the model’s interconnection structure to be physically dynamic. Thus, the implementations address several major parts of a neural simulation, including the organization of connections as well as the arithmetic performed on them.

To compare performance, the authors implement a Hopfield model using each approach at six model sizes while holding the number of Connection Machine processors the same. This makes model size and implementation strategy the central dimensions of the comparison. The contribution is a pair of concrete mappings from neural computation to a parallel machine, together with a structured comparison of how those mappings perform.
neurips-1987-neural-network-implementati.tldr: Two Connection Machine implementations parallelize neural computation and are compared using Hopfield models at six sizes.

paragraphs: The paper starts from the observation that interactions among tropisms can explain apparently complex biological behavior. A tropism is a response tendency associated with a stimulus. When several such tendencies act together, their combined effect can produce responses to combinations of environmental signals that seem much more elaborate than the individual tendencies.

The authors propose generalizing this idea into a computational approach called tropistic processing. The abstract states that this generalization supports efficient implementations of effective algorithms that respond to changing environmental conditions. The central design idea is to build useful behavior from interacting response tendencies.

The paper presents applications in simulated behavior synthesis, path planning, clustering, and engineering design optimization. These examples connect the same processing idea to generating actions, organizing patterns, and searching for designs. Their breadth is part of the motivation: a principle drawn from biological responses is presented as a reusable algorithmic approach. The stated contribution is the generalization and its applications, with intelligent-looking adaptation explained through the interaction of simpler responses.
neurips-1987-on-tropistic-processing-and.tldr: Tropistic processing builds adaptive algorithms from interacting stimulus-response tendencies, with applications from path planning to design optimization.

paragraphs: This paper gives general formulas for translating optimization problems into ordinary differential equations associated with artificial neural networks. A candidate solution becomes a system state, and optimization is studied through the state’s evolution. The authors compare these neural dynamical systems with systems based on gradient search.

The comparison measures settling time from an initial state to a target state. A simple analytical example shows a case where the neural-network formulation would settle faster. This establishes that the choice of dynamics can favor a neural formulation in at least one explicitly examined situation.

A more complicated simulated problem produces the opposite outcome. The task simplifies the medical-imaging problem of locating cerebral activity from electromagnetic measurements at the scalp. In those simulations, gradient-based systems typically settle 50 to 100 times faster than the neural optimization systems considered. Taken together, the results show why a favorable analytical example cannot determine practical performance across problems. The mapping principle provides a construction method, while the comparison makes settling behavior an essential part of evaluating that construction.
neurips-1987-optimization-with-artificia.tldr: The paper maps optimization into neural dynamics, but its imaging simulations find gradient-based systems typically settle 50–100 times faster.

paragraphs: Associative memories that continually learn and forget raise evaluation questions beyond how much information they can store at once. The paper considers modifications of the McCulloch/Pitts model with both processes. If such a network avoids saturation, learning updates can continue indefinitely, making its behavior over continuing use central to its assessment.

Saturation here means an overload of information that prevents the memory from functioning effectively. Because learning and forgetting change what the network retains, a single information-capacity measure is insufficient to compare these systems. The authors introduce mathematical quantities for network plasticity, the efficacy of an information vector, and the probability of saturation.

These quantities provide additional ways to characterize a memory and support analytical comparisons between different networks. The approach matters because ongoing learning requires attention to adaptation, the usefulness of stored information, and the risk of overload together. The paper’s contribution is a more suitable evaluation framework for memories whose contents keep changing, with continued updating explicitly dependent on avoiding saturation.
neurips-1987-performance-measures-for-as.tldr: The paper defines measures beyond storage capacity to compare associative memories that continually learn and forget.

paragraphs: The paper evaluates bidirectional associative memories using successful recall in a synchronous discrete model. It examines 100 random memories of size 64 by 64 while varying the number of stored vectors. Their observed capacity falls well below the cited upper bound based on the smaller of the two layer dimensions.

On average, these memories achieve about 68% of the capacity of a Hopfield memory with the same number of neurons. Orthonormal coding increases effective storage capacity by only 25%. The authors attribute the restriction to spurious stable states: the network can settle into states that interfere with the intended recall.

The proposed remedy replaces thresholding in the back layer with a nonlinear process called Dominant Label Selection. This can avoid spurious stable states. Its simplest form, a winner-take-all network, is sensitive to faults, so the authors discuss orthogonal or unitary transformations to improve fault tolerance. A Fourier transform implemented by a lens supplies an optical example. The work connects a measured recall limitation with a change to the memory’s update mechanism.
neurips-1987-reflexive-associative-memor.tldr: Bidirectional memories show limited recall capacity, motivating Dominant Label Selection to avoid spurious stable states.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an efficient method for creating self-organizing associative databases. These databases associate inputs with outputs, making the relationship between an observed input and its corresponding response the central function. The work connects this idea to robot eyesight systems, where visual information must support useful recognition or behavior.

The first part develops the self-organization algorithm. The abstract also describes the resulting arrangement as a new style of neural network when viewed from a hardware perspective. This gives the proposal both an algorithmic side, concerning how associations become organized, and an implementation side, concerning the network that embodies those associations.

The second part demonstrates applicability to handwritten-letter recognition and an autonomous mobile robot system. These examples place the associative database in both a recognition task and a robotic setting. The contribution is therefore a self-organization method accompanied by demonstrations of use. Its relevance lies in connecting a general input-output association mechanism to concrete visual applications, including the perceptual needs of an autonomous robot.
neurips-1987-self-organization-of-associ.tldr: A self-organizing associative database is proposed and demonstrated in handwritten-letter recognition and an autonomous mobile robot system.

paragraphs: This paper builds a computer model of a hippocampal pyramidal cell by combining data from several sources. The goal is a consistent description of this cell type that can connect its electrical behavior with possible information-processing functions. The model includes eleven nonlinear currents associated with the soma, or cell body.

The neuron’s electrical structure is represented using a soma/short-cable approximation. This provides a simplified spatial description alongside the detailed collection of currents. The combination allows simulations to investigate how the modeled electrical mechanisms contribute to the behavior of the cell as a whole.

The simulations reproduce a broad range of somatic electrical behavior, with agreement described as qualitative or quantitative depending on the behavior. They also demonstrate possible information-processing roles for the different currents. Reproducing observed electrical behavior makes the model useful for exploring those roles, while the wording remains appropriately tentative: the simulations suggest functional interpretations. The contribution is a unified cell model that brings multiple electrical mechanisms into a common account and uses them to investigate computation within a neuron.
neurips-1987-simulations-suggest-informa.tldr: A hippocampal cell model reproduces diverse electrical behaviors and suggests information-processing roles for eleven nonlinear somatic currents.

paragraphs: The paper studies how spatial organization affects a neural network under Markovian assumptions about cells and their connections. This is motivated by image modeling and pattern analysis, where computations involve spatially distributed, uncertain signals. The authors first construct a random neural-network model and examine its organization through discrete-event simulation.

They then investigate an analytical description based on product-form queueing networks. In this representation, moving customers stand for stimulations, and routing probabilities describe connections between nodes. Different rules governing how long a stimulation remains at a node let the model represent different processing disciplines.

The authors obtain solutions under these disciplines and study how excitation is distributed across the network. They examine the effects of network topology and the arrival pattern of external stimulation, comparing analytical results with simulation measurements. The reported agreement validates the approach in the studied setting. The contribution is a bridge between stochastic neural modeling and queueing theory, making spatial excitation patterns accessible through both simulation and mathematical analysis.
neurips-1987-spatial-organization-of-neu.tldr: A queueing-network formulation analytically describes excitation in random neural networks, with simulation comparisons supporting the approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies speech vocabularies that are harder to distinguish than isolated digits. One is the alphabetic E-set, whose members have weak distinguishing cues. The other contains polysyllabic words, where variation in timing makes recognition difficult. These two tasks expose different obstacles that a speech-recognition system must address.

For polysyllabic words, the authors use a time pre-alignment technique based on dynamic programming. This addresses timing variation before recognition. For the E-set, they improve performance by focusing attention, directing the recognition process toward the information needed to distinguish similar inputs.

Both vocabularies achieve recognition accuracy above 98% with a single-layer perceptron. The result connects a relatively simple classifier with processing choices tailored to the source of difficulty in each vocabulary. Timing alignment helps with variation across longer words, while attention helps with weak discriminating information. The stated findings show that these targeted techniques can support highly accurate recognition on the two vocabularies studied, making the treatment of the input central to the system’s success.
neurips-1987-speech-recognition-experime.tldr: Time alignment and focused attention enable single-layer perceptrons to exceed 98% recognition accuracy on two difficult speech vocabularies.

paragraphs: The paper develops a qualitative theory of Hopfield networks using results about large interconnected dynamical systems. It views a network as many individual neurons linked together. The resulting analysis expresses network behavior through properties of the neurons and the structure of their interconnections.

Several questions concern what happens near an equilibrium, a state that remains unchanged under the network dynamics. The paper addresses asymptotic stability, exponential stability, and instability. These distinguish whether nearby states approach an equilibrium, whether that approach has an exponential rate, or whether the equilibrium fails to retain nearby trajectories.

The analysis also estimates bounds on trajectories and the domain of attraction of a stable equilibrium: the set of starting states that move toward it. Finally, it considers stability when network structure is perturbed. Together, these results connect local component properties with the behavior of the complete system. This provides a mathematical framework for asking where a network can move, which states it can settle into, and how those conclusions depend on its connections.
neurips-1987-stability-results-for-neura.tldr: The paper analyzes Hopfield-network stability through individual neuron properties and the structure of their interconnections.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a probabilistic interpretation of supervised neural-network learning. It treats the values of both input and output neurons as probabilities. That interpretation makes uncertain information part of the model’s basic meaning, which is useful when observations or desired responses are imperfect.

The proposed learning objective is log likelihood. Connection weights change in the gradient direction that makes the supervised information more probable under the network. This reframes back-propagation around a statistical objective and connects the interpretation of neural values directly to the quantity optimized during learning.

The authors argue that this perspective generalizes back-propagation and gives it a stronger conceptual foundation. They also suggest that it could improve efficiency, presenting that benefit as a possibility. The motivation includes applications such as text-to-phoneme mapping, illness diagnosis, and sonar-target classification, where probabilistic information can be natural. The contribution described is the proposed learning formulation: probabilities define what neural values mean, and likelihood defines how the network should adjust its connections to fit supervised evidence.
neurips-1987-supervised-learning-of-prob.tldr: The paper proposes probabilistic inputs and outputs with log-likelihood learning as a principled generalization of back-propagation.

paragraphs: Alternating projection neural networks operate by repeatedly projecting between two or more constraint sets. This gives their behavior a geometric interpretation in signal space. The paper uses that interpretation to establish criteria for convergence to a desired, unique result and considers both homogeneous and layered network organizations.

The reported storage capacity is on the order of the combined number of input and hidden neurons. For a trained layered network with binary output neurons, the architecture can be configured to converge in one iteration. More generally, the abstract describes an exponential convergence rate.

The authors identify sigmoid-type nonlinearities, network relaxation, and additional hidden neurons as ways to improve convergence. They also show that responses to inputs outside the training set can be evaluated analytically. The approach therefore links architecture, convergence, storage, and generalization within a common mathematical description. Its significance is that network behavior can be studied through the geometry of the constraints, including a particularly strong convergence result for the stated binary-output setting.
neurips-1987-the-performance-of-convex-s.tldr: Alternating projection networks make convergence and generalization analytically tractable, with one-iteration convergence possible for trained layered networks with binary outputs.

paragraphs: The paper proposes that each stage of a perceptual network should preserve as much information about its input as possible. It expresses this goal by maximizing a Shannon information rate between the stage’s input and output. The optimization explicitly includes constraints and processing noise, so preservation is considered within the conditions the stage must operate under.

For simple model cases, the author derives consequences of this principle and discusses an algorithmic implementation. The analysis explores how an information-preservation objective could lead to biologically relevant features, including topographic maps, distortions of those maps, orientation selectivity, and extraction of spatial and temporal correlations.

This gives a common organizing question to several aspects of perceptual architecture: which transformation retains the most useful input information under the stated constraints and noise? The results are presented for simple cases, and the architectural implications are described as possibilities. The paper also suggests a connection with minimum entropy production in nonequilibrium thermodynamics, extending the proposed principle into a broader theoretical discussion.
neurips-1987-towards-an-organizing-princ.tldr: Maximizing information preservation under noise and constraints is proposed as an organizing principle for layered perceptual networks.
